title: SPORK: Self-Speculative Forking to Accelerate Agentic LLM Inference
hook: An agent's tool-call loop idles the GPU 16-37% of the time waiting on results. SPORK has the model predict its own next tool call early enough to start it before reasoning even finishes.
key_points: A probe forked at the start of generation predicts Qwen3-32B's upcoming tool name with 74.6-99.6% accuracy.
SPORK dispatches the speculated tool call early, overlapping its execution with the remaining chain-of-thought decode.
Training-free: no auxiliary predictor model, historical traces, or static workflow graph — a thin controller over completion APIs.
On rejection it falls back to serial execution with no correctness penalty; rejected probes recycle as speculative-decoding drafts.
Cuts Qwen3-32B's GAIA P95 latency by 18% (131.9s to 108.1s), holding across 4B-32B dense and MoE models.
content_html: LLM agents that reason, call a tool, then wait, waste a lot of GPU time doing it: 16-37% of wall time in the authors' own workloads. SPORK's trick is to have the model predict its own next tool call early enough to start it before reasoning even finishes.
extra_html:
How it works

A probe forked at the start of generation predicts Qwen3-32B's upcoming tool name with 74.6-99.6% accuracy across five benchmarks — good enough that SPORK dispatches the guessed tool call immediately, overlapping its execution with the rest of the chain-of-thought decode. A cost model decides when speculation is worth it, a confidence gate filters out likely mispredictions, and if a probe turns out wrong, its partial tokens get reused as a speculative-decoding draft instead of being thrown away. On acceptance the tool result is often ready by the time reasoning ends; on rejection, SPORK just falls back to normal serial execution with no accuracy cost.

Why it matters

It's training-free — no auxiliary predictor model, no historical traces, no static workflow graph, just a thin controller sitting over standard completion APIs, so it deploys day one. On real-tool benchmarks it cuts Qwen3-32B's GAIA P95 latency by 18% (131.9s to 108.1s), holds up across model sizes from 4B to 32B and across dense and mixture-of-experts models, and keeps task accuracy within 1 percentage point of baseline or better everywhere it was measured. It's also orthogonal to token-level speculative decoding, so the two can stack. Bai and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

flashcards.prompt: What's the key insight behind SPORK's speculation?
flashcards.back_html: The model can predict its own next tool call: a probe forked at the start of generation predicts it with 74.6-99.6% accuracy, so SPORK can dispatch that tool call before reasoning finishes.

flashcards.prompt: What happens when SPORK's forked probe mispredicts the tool call?

choices.text: It falls back to normal serial execution with no correctness penalty, and can reuse the probe's partial tokens as a speculative-decoding draft
The agent's answer is discarded and the task fails
It silently keeps the wrong tool call result and continues

flashcards.explanation_html: On rejection SPORK just executes serially as usual; the failed probe isn't wasted since its tokens can double as a speculative-decoding draft.

flashcards.prompt: Why is SPORK described as 'training-free' and deployable day one?
flashcards.back_html: It needs no auxiliary predictor model, no historical usage traces, and no static workflow graph — just a thin controller layered over standard completion APIs.
